extracted.intended_audience: education researchers, edtech developers, instructors, and policymakers interested in AI in education
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate how AI is applied across education (administration, instruction, learning), including impacts, system forms (ITS, AIWBES/IWBE, cobots, VR), benefits, and risks. Useful for assessing educational AI systems or designing studies of AI in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of AI in educational scenarios (administration, instruction, learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI provides different functions in educational scenarios, typically grouped into administration, instruction, and learning (Tab. 2 shows the different functions AI can work as in education scenarios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite functional framing to categorize system capabilities and to evaluate scope of impact (e.g., whether a system only automates admin vs. supports pedagogy and student learning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration: automation of administrative tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can automate administrative tasks such as students' assignments and papers reviews, grading, and providing feedback to students; automate management and administrative functions in academic institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the system provides grading, plagiarism checking, feedback generation, or other management features (examples: Knewton, TurnItIn, Ecree, Grammarly). Consider measured gains in efficiency and workload reduction for instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction: AI as pedagogical tool
rubrics_metrics.description: AI is used as a pedagogical or instructional tool (simulation-based instruction, intelligent tutoring, VR/3-D, cobots/chatbots) that can improve instructional quality and support teacher-like functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of simulation/VR, ITS, conversational agents, robots or chatbot features, and whether these support curriculum delivery and pedagogical strategies (examples: ACTIVE Math, MATHia, Why2Atlas, Comet, Viper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning: personalization and customization of content
rubrics_metrics.description: AI enables customization and personalization of curriculum and content aligned with learners' needs, abilities, and capabilities, improving uptake and retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge systems by their ability to profile learners and adapt content in real time (examples: Knewton, Cerego, Immersive Reader, CALL). Metrics include personalization granularity and demonstrated learning gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent/adaptive web-based education (AIWBES/IWBE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration of AI principles into web-based learning platforms (AIWBES / IWBE) that consider learner knowledge, skills, performance, compatibilities and model social agents (teachers, students) to create robust interactive adaptive systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate multi-agent design, learner modeling, adaptivity across contexts, and accessibility (examples: adaptive hypermedia, information filtering, StudentTracker middleware).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness, efficiency, and quality (operational definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the paper: efficiency = delivery of relevant content in line with curriculum and learner needs; effectiveness = attainment (uptake and retention) of learning objectives; quality = overall instructional standard and alignment to curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing systems, apply these operational definitions: measure time/resource savings (efficiency), student learning outcomes (effectiveness), and curriculum alignment/coverage (quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) features and evidence-based practice
rubrics_metrics.description: ITS leverage evidence-based practices including cognition and learning models, conversational/animated agents, and probing strategies to promote deep learning (e.g., AutoTutor, DeepTutor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ITS by their pedagogical model fidelity (how they probe, scaffold, and provide feedback), empirical evidence of learning gains, and presence of learner-centered personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation, virtual reality (VR), and 3-D technology for experiential learning
rubrics_metrics.description: VR and 3-D simulation enable experiential learning and practical exposure, improving usability, enjoyment, learner enthusiasm, motivation, and increased interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fidelity of simulation, alignment to learning objectives, and measured affective and cognitive outcomes (engagement, retention, transfer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cobots/humanoid robots and conversational agents as teaching assistants
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration of AI into robots (cobots) and chatbots endowed with cognitive, decision-making, dialogue and conversational abilities to undertake teaching tasks or routine queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess naturalness and pedagogical value of interactions, ability to support or augment instructors, and evidence for learning benefits (examples discussed: cobots, chatbots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment and grading automation (including computer vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI is used to grade homework and essays, evaluate exams (including image-based handwritten papers via computer vision), and provide grading guides and feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accuracy, reliability, transparency of automated assessment, alignment to rubrics/benchmarks, ability to handle varied responses, and impacts on instructor time allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic integrity risks and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: AI tools can both support academic integrity (plagiarism detection, proctoring) and threaten it (facilitating cheating via paper mills, paper churning); there are trade-offs to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems for anti-cheating safeguards, misuse risk, and whether they introduce new integrity vulnerabilities; consider both proctoring tools (TurnItIn, WhiteSmoke) and emerging abuse vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access, affordability, and scalability (global access to learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-enabled web-based platforms can eliminate barriers to learning (national/international borders), foster global access and affordability, and be accessible from anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reach, language/support for diverse learners, cost implications, and infrastructural requirements for equitable access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and learning analytics (tracking progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI tracks learning progression (knowledge, understanding, completed activities, time) and uses this to adapt pedagogy and content (e.g., StudentTracker middleware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the granularity of analytics, predictive power, transparency to stakeholders, and how analytics inform instructional decisions and personalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias, fairness, and reduction of human bias
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems can reduce human bias in grading by applying preset rubrics and benchmarks, but human bias remains an emerging issue requiring attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fairness audits, bias-mitigation strategies, transparency of models, and whether automated grading actually reduces or exacerbates disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student performance improvement and personalized pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can detect student learning shortcomings early, tailor teaching methods to individual strengths/personality, predict career paths, and recommend course selections to improve outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accuracy of diagnostics, effectiveness of personalized interventions, and ethical/privacy considerations of career prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement strategies including gamification
rubrics_metrics.description: Gamification and related interactive technologies (simulation, team-viewer applications) are used alongside AI to improve engagement and instructional effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess design of gamified elements, alignment with learning goals, and measured effects on motivation and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary design and development teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and implementation of AI in education brings together system designers, data scientists, product designers, statisticians, linguists, cognitive scientists, psychologists, and education experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether development involves appropriate multidisciplinary expertise, which impacts system validity, pedagogical soundness, and adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs: positive effects vs. negative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature indicates that positive effects (improved efficiency, effectiveness, access, personalization) generally outweigh negatives (integrity threats, bias), but trade-offs exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating AI interventions consider both benefits and downsides, require empirical evidence for claimed improvements, and document mitigation strategies for harms.
